_doc: Single source of truth for slide-native companion figures. R (05c/05d) reads layout + export dims to build output/figures/slides/. The deck generator reads headline/annotation/source/bullets. See Infrastructure/specs/2026-07-09_slide-native-figures.md.
_source_default: Source: Economic Innovation Group 80-80 wage subsidy simulation, 2026.

fig01_subsidy_schedule.headline: The subsidy fills 80% of the gap to a $16.80 target — in every paycheck.
fig01_subsidy_schedule.annotation: Target = 80% of the $21.00 paid-hourly median; $7.25 is the lowest creditable base wage.

fig02_cost_waterfall.headline: Taxes and safety-net savings cut the cost from $56B gross to $45B net.
fig02_cost_waterfall.annotation: Recaptured taxes and SNAP/Medicaid savings, partly offset by higher ACA premium credits.

fig13_cost_band.headline: Only wholesale wage renegotiation escapes the $45–48B net range.
fig13_cost_band.annotation: Static, reduced-form, and structural models all cluster in the $45–48B net range.

fig03_takeup_by_group.headline: It reaches deepest among women, the young, and the least credentialed.
fig03_takeup_by_group.annotation: Dashed line: overall take-up, 21.7% of the paid-hourly workforce.
bullets: Women: 26.2% take-up vs. 17.2% for men; women are 60.5% of recipients.
Ages 16–24: 43.0% qualify — the highest take-up of any group.
Less than high school: 37.4% vs. 6.8% with a graduate degree.
Single parents: 23.5% qualify, above married parents (13.5%).

fig04_subsidy_by_wage.headline: The lowest-wage workers receive the largest checks — by construction.
fig04_subsidy_by_wage.annotation: Average annual subsidy runs from $10,281 at $7.25–9 down to $2,206 at $13–16.80.

fig05_avg_subsidy_by_state.headline: Because the target is national, money flows to lagging labor markets.
fig05_avg_subsidy_by_state.annotation: Average annual subsidy per eligible worker, by state.
bullets: Louisiana $4,981 and Mississippi $4,990 per eligible worker.
No commission picks winners — the formula finds distressed places.

fig06_reservation_wage.section: Does it pull people into work?
fig06_reservation_wage.headline: The subsidy exists to clear a worker's entry threshold.
fig06_reservation_wage.annotation: The employer's offer alone falls short; the subsidy lifts total pay over the worker's reservation wage.

fig07_entry_band_by_cell.section: Does it pull people into work?
fig07_entry_band_by_cell.headline: Entry by group, benchmarked against the closest real-world precedents.
fig07_entry_band_by_cell.annotation: 1.49M central (floor 1.02M, high 3.81M) — between Paycheck Plus and the Self-Sufficiency Project.

fig07b_entrants_by_status.section: Does it pull people into work?
fig07b_entrants_by_status.headline: The entrants are mostly job-seekers — not the disabled or retired.
fig07b_entrants_by_status.annotation: About a third are unemployed searchers; the disabled and retired are ~3% of entrants.

fig08_pool_wage_distribution.section: Does it pull people into work?
fig08_pool_wage_distribution.headline: Most non-workers could still command offers above the target.
fig08_pool_wage_distribution.annotation: 47.8% of the pool draws offers below $16.80, vs. 21.7% of paid-hourly workers.

fig09_firm_capture.headline: Employers keep about 3% of the subsidy under realistic wage stickiness.
fig09_firm_capture.annotation: No more than ~4% across bargaining assumptions; the $7.25 floor caps how far wages can fall.

fig10_cost_per_job.headline: Cost per new job undercuts the job-creation policies we already run.
fig10_cost_per_job.annotation: ~$5,300 marginal; ~$32K fully loaded vs. $154K+ Buy American and ~$900K steel tariffs.

fig11_benefit_cliff.headline: The subsidy has no cliff of its own — but it inherits everyone else's.
fig11_benefit_cliff.annotation: Net income climbs with earnings, then drops where Medicaid and other benefits phase out.

fig11b_net_income_by_hours.headline: Past ~53 hours a week, the clawback can swallow the subsidy.
fig11b_net_income_by_hours.annotation: The subsidy adds ~$7,800 net at 20 hrs/wk and ~$5,600 at 40; it caps at 2,080 hours a year.

fig12_clawback_net_gain.headline: Single mothers gain the least net value from working — half is clawed back.
fig12_clawback_net_gain.annotation: Median net return to working rises ~18% for single mothers vs. ~27% and ~23% for others.

fig14_mpl_uncertainty.headline: Entry spans 0.23–3.81M; the wage penalty is the single largest lever.
bullets: Cost is the firm result: $45–48B net across all three models.
Entry is the wider band — drivers vary jointly, not one at a time.
Drivers: participation elasticity, offer dispersion, wage penalty.
Headline = evidence-central; a zero wage penalty is the setting the evidence rules out.

fig15_hours_margin.headline: A second margin: part-timers add up to ~280K full-time-equivalents.
fig15_hours_margin.annotation: Consensus elasticities (0.2–0.33) give 0.19–0.28M FTE, alongside ~0.7M FTE from entry.

figA1_wage_distribution.headline: About one in five paid-hourly workers earn below the target.
figA1_wage_distribution.annotation: Reported wages heap on round-dollar values; the $16.80 target sits on a dense stretch.
